---
title: "Concept map"
description: "How gauge balancing and coordinated rounding answer different quantization questions."
---

## One product, two control points

Suppose two matrices are multiplied through an inner dimension and then stored
on scalar grids. There are two distinct moments at which the computation can be
changed.

1. **Before quantization:** apply a product-preserving inner transformation to
   redistribute energy and coordinate ranges while leaving the exact product
   unchanged.
2. **At rounding time:** keep the grid fixed but coordinate up/down decisions so
   their product errors cancel in a low-dimensional output image.

The first experiment family studies limits under independent scalar noise. The
second studies deterministic coordination after the fractional residues and an
output block are known.

## Three quantities that must not be conflated

| Quantity | Question |
| --- | --- |
| Factorization energy | How much squared factor energy is needed to represent a fixed product? |
| Coordinate range | How much larger is the scalar grid step than an average-energy scale? |
| Product discrepancy | How much can signed rounding errors cancel after multiplication? |

Balancing can close an energy gap without making every coordinate equally
small. Flattening addresses that second range gap. Coordinated rounding is a
different mechanism: it exploits the rank and row sensitivities of the current
output block.

## Evidence types

Exact identities, deterministic certificates, seeded numerical studies, and
wall-clock measurements are labeled separately. A failed sufficient
certificate means that benefit is not certified; it is not evidence that a
particular unmodeled mechanism caused the failure.

Continue with [gauge balancing](tutorials/nuclear-floor.qmd) or
[coordinated rounding](tutorials/coordinated-rounding.qmd).
